title: Tight and bright
caption: The globular cluster Messier 70, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M 70 · constellation Sagittarius · about 30000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The compact, brilliant centre of the globular cluster Messier 70 fills this Hubble image, the cluster growing steadily brighter toward its middle. Globular clusters are tight quarters, where gravity binds hundreds of thousands of stars into a small region of space.

Messier 70 is special because it has undergone core collapse. As stars in a cluster interact over time, lighter ones tend to speed up and wander toward the edges, while heavier ones slow down and gather in orbits near the centre. That huddling creates the dense, bright cores typical of core-collapsed clusters. Of the Milky Way's more than 150 globulars, roughly one in five has been through it.

While many globular clusters live in the galaxy's outskirts, this one circles near the heart of the Milky Way, around 30 000 light-years from the Solar System. It has stayed intact despite the strong gravitational pull of the galactic hub.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.37 x 3.43 arcminutes) and distance (30000 light years), the frame spans roughly 29 × 30 light-years. Its light set out about 30,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through binoculars Messier 70 is only very faintly visible, but Hubble resolves the individual stars of its crowded core.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Just about 68 light-years wide, Messier 70 can be glimpsed, very faintly, with binoculars under dark skies in Sagittarius. Charles Messier logged it in 1780, making it number seventy in his famous list. The picture comes from the Advanced Camera for Surveys and covers about 3.3 by 3.3 arcminutes.
alt: The bright, compact centre of a globular cluster, growing brighter toward the middle.
